transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I came in because... I know my in-laws aren't just having normal arguments with me anymore. It's gone way past that. They are actually using the altar and the parish committee to push me out. They're trying to make everyone forget what I have done for this family over the years. So, that's what's going on, and that's why I'm here.
How long have you felt that your in-laws and the parish committee have been working together to push you out?
Well, it's been... I'd say about two months now. This whole crisis really started right after we had a big fight—my in-laws and I—over the Día de los Muertos altar. That's when it all began.

Over these past two months, have you also noticed changes in your mood or energy—like feeling unusually elevated, irritable, or excessively sad or hopeless—that happen along with these concerns about your in-laws?

Well, yes, I suppose. There were days recently when I just felt... I don't know, so bright and certain about everything I was doing. But then, if anyone even questioned me about the altar, I would just snap at them. I would get so mad, it felt like they were insulting my whole family. So yes, I have definitely been a lot more irritable lately.
Even on days when you don't feel that unusual brightness or irritability, do you still believe your in-laws and the parish committee are conspiring against you?

Well... it changes. The really intense parts—like hearing voices and actually seeing my mother—that only happened during that time when I was barely sleeping. I was just rushing around everywhere, feeling so sure I had this special duty to fix the altar. When my mood dropped after that... I mean, I still felt really guilty and sad, but I wasn't hearing or seeing those things anymore.

Thinking about times when your mood has been completely normal—not unusually high, irritable, or low—do you still find yourself believing that your in-laws and the parish committee are conspiring against you?

No, not really. When my mood is just... normal, I don't think about them conspiring against me. Like I said before, the really strange things—hearing the voices, seeing my mother—that only happened when I was barely sleeping and rushing around, feeling like I had this special duty to fix the altar. Once that stopped and my mood dropped, I just felt guilty and sad. But I wasn't hearing or seeing those things anymore, and I didn't feel like everyone was out to get me.

latest_inference.note: Psychotic symptoms (voices, seeing mother, paranoid beliefs about in-laws) occurred only during the manic episode with sleeplessness/elevated mood, and resolved once mood normalized or shifted to depression—patient denies persecutory beliefs during euthymic periods. This absence of psychosis independent of mood episodes argues against schizoaffective disorder (F25), which requires psychotic symptoms for a substantial period without mood symptoms. This supports Bipolar I disorder with mood-congruent/incongruent psychotic features instead.

This pattern is consistent with Bipolar I Disorder, current episode manic, severe with psychotic symptoms (F31.2).
